candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'count something nobody counts', with the home care worker viewpoint and 'the first minute', suggested counting hearing aids that work rather than hearing aids present, and putting the aid in before the conversation starts.
candidates.working_title: Count the hearing aids that work
candidates.core_insight: A care record that says a person has a hearing aid does not show whether it works, and a short daily check of battery, switch and programme, tubing or dome, and wax guard catches the common faults.
candidates.angle: Care homes, wards and home care records note whether a person owns a hearing aid. In a US nursing home survey, most residents who used hearing aids had problems with them, most needed help to look after them, and close to half of staff had no training in their use or care. The count that would change care is the number of aids that worked this morning. The order of events in a care visit is the practical detail: aid in and glasses on first, then the conversation.
candidates.position: Care settings should check every day that hearing aids work, record the result, and train staff to do it, rather than recording only that a person has one.
claims_needing_evidence: Among nursing home residents who used hearing aids, a majority of those with information (69%) had problems with the devices, 86% needed help to care for them, and close to half of staff had received no training in hearing aid use or maintenance (Cohen-Mansfield and Taylor 2004, J Am Med Dir Assoc, Part 2; abstract read in PubMed, full text to check).
Gross hearing impairment was undetected in clinical practice in over half of residents of one large nursing home (Cohen-Mansfield and Taylor 2004, Part 1; abstract read).

Common hearing aid faults that staff can check for include a flat battery, the aid switched off or on the wrong programme, blocked tubing or dome, and a blocked wax guard (NHS audiology or British Academy of Audiology hearing aid care guidance; check source).
A listening check or a basic daily check can be taught to care staff (care home training resource or study; check before using).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'examine a neglected consequence', with the first-month timescale, pointed to the weeks after a hearing aid is fitted, when unexpected loudness or discomfort leads some people to stop wearing it.
candidates.working_title: The first weeks with new hearing aids
candidates.core_insight: New hearing aids often sound loud or strange at first and many problems can be fixed at a follow-up appointment, so people should go back and ask for adjustments rather than put the aids in a drawer.
candidates.angle: Services treat fitting as the end of the pathway. For the person, the first weeks are when the decision to keep wearing the aids is made. Everyday sounds that have not been heard for years come back, and some aids hurt or whistle. Guidance recommends a follow-up appointment after fitting, and that is the moment to say what is wrong.
candidates.position: People with new hearing aids should expect a settling-in period, attend the follow-up appointment and report problems; services should make that follow-up easy to get.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE NG98 recommends a follow-up audiology appointment 6 to 12 weeks after hearing aids are fitted (NICE NG98 text; check wording and timing).

A substantial proportion of people who own hearing aids do not wear them regularly, with reasons including fit and comfort, sound quality, background noise and difficulty handling them (systematic review, e.g. McCormack and Fortnum 2013, Int J Audiol; check).
People newly fitted with hearing aids commonly notice everyday sounds as louder or unfamiliar in the first weeks (NHS audiology patient information or acclimatisation research; check).
Hearing aid settings and fittings can be adjusted after fitting in response to the wearer's reports (NHS audiology information).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'apply it to the poorest or most isolated person', with the kettle, suggested a person living alone with serious sight loss making a hot drink, and the council vision rehabilitation that teaches daily tasks and supplies simple equipment such as a liquid level indicator.
candidates.working_title: Sight loss certification can bring help at home
candidates.core_insight: People with serious sight loss can be certified as sight impaired or severely sight impaired by an eye consultant, which can lead to a council assessment and vision rehabilitation that teaches safer ways to cook, move around and read, with equipment such as liquid level indicators and talking clocks.
candidates.angle: Eye clinics measure and treat eyes. Living alone with sight loss is a set of daily tasks: making a hot drink, crossing a road, reading post, telling tablets apart. Rehabilitation workers teach those tasks. The person most dependent on this help is the one with nobody at home, and the route to it often starts with a form the eye clinic completes.
candidates.position: People with serious sight loss, especially those living alone, should be offered certification and referral for vision rehabilitation; they and their families can ask for both.
claims_needing_evidence: In England, a consultant ophthalmologist completes a Certificate of Vision Impairment (CVI), which is sent with consent to the person's council and can lead to registration and an assessment of needs (Department of Health and Social Care CVI explanatory notes; Scotland uses a separate CVI Scotland form; check both).
Councils provide or arrange vision rehabilitation, which can include mobility training, daily living skills and equipment (Care Act 2014 statutory guidance; Scottish equivalent; check).

Certification or registration can give access to some concessions, such as Blue Badge eligibility and a TV licence reduction for people certified severely sight impaired (official sources; check each before naming).
Some people eligible for certification are never certified (UK study of under-certification; check before using).
Liquid level indicators and talking clocks are available through sensory services and sight loss charities (council or charity equipment information).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find an outcome that patients value and the routine measure misses', with 'visibility', led to the gap between letters read on a chart in a bright clinic and the things people say they want to see again.
candidates.working_title: Cataract surgery and what the letter chart misses
candidates.core_insight: Cataract surgery is often judged by the letter chart, but people also care about glare, dim light, faces, steps and reading, and a short UK questionnaire asks about eyesight in daily life.
candidates.angle: A letter chart in a bright room measures one thing well. Cataract also causes glare from headlights and low sun, washed-out contrast and trouble in dim light. A five-item UK questionnaire, Cat-PROM5, asks people about their own eyesight in daily life and changes a great deal after surgery. Before surgery, the useful question is what the person can no longer do; after surgery, the useful follow-up is whether it has come back.
candidates.position: Decisions about cataract surgery, and judgements of its success, should include how eyesight affects the person's daily life, and not rest on the letter chart alone.
claims_needing_evidence: Cat-PROM5 is a five-item patient-reported outcome measure for cataract surgery, developed in 822 UK patients awaiting surgery, with high responsiveness to surgery (Sparrow et al. 2018, Eye; abstract read in PubMed).
Cataract reduces contrast sensitivity and increases glare disability, which high-contrast letter charts can underestimate (ophthalmology review; check).
NICE NG77 recommends that the decision to refer for cataract surgery takes account of the impact on the person's daily life and quality of life (NICE NG77; check wording).
The UK National Ophthalmology Database cataract audit reports visual acuity and complication outcomes (RCOphth NOD annual report; check whether patient-reported outcomes are included).

candidates.gain: Words for describing how cataract affects daily life, and a reason to say it.
candidates.follow: It separates what services count from what people live with.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'reverse the default assumption', with 'habit' and 'five years', led to the habit of waiting years until hearing is bad before seeking help, set against trial evidence in mild to moderate loss.
candidates.working_title: Mild hearing loss is worth treating
candidates.core_insight: Trials in adults with mild to moderate hearing loss found that hearing aids likely give a large improvement in everyday listening and hearing-related quality of life, so people do not need to wait until hearing is severe to ask for help.
candidates.angle: A common assumption is that hearing aids are for people who hear very little. The 2026 Cochrane update pooled trials of people with mild to moderate loss and found a large benefit for everyday listening and hearing-related quality of life, with moderate certainty. The same review did not find clear effects on loneliness or working memory, which keeps the promise accurate: hearing aids help hearing.
candidates.position: Adults who notice hearing difficulty should ask for a hearing assessment now rather than waiting until the loss is severe.
claims_needing_evidence: The 2026 Cochrane update (16 RCTs, 2261 participants, mild to moderate hearing loss) found hearing aids likely produce a large improvement in hearing-specific health-related quality of life and listening ability, with moderate-certainty evidence (Ferguson et al. 2026; abstract read in PubMed).
The same review found little to no difference in loneliness (low certainty) and very uncertain evidence on working memory (Ferguson et al. 2026; abstract read).
People in the UK typically wait years between noticing hearing difficulty and getting hearing aids (Davis et al. 2007 HTA or later UK study; check the figure before using any number).
NHS hearing assessments and hearing aids are provided free of charge (NHS source).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the viewpoint to someone else in the scene' moved the view from the clinician to the patient's chair, where a face in front of a bright window is in shadow and a head turned to the screen gives nothing to lip-read.
candidates.working_title: The view from the patient's chair
candidates.core_insight: People with hearing loss rely on seeing the speaker's face, so sitting with your back to a window, turning to the screen while talking, or covering your mouth removes information they use to understand speech.
candidates.angle: The clinician sees a well-lit patient. The patient may see a dark outline against the window and, at the moment the plan is explained, the side of a head turned to the computer. Seeing the talker's face improves understanding of speech in noise substantially. Moving the chair so light falls on your face, and saying the plan before or after typing, costs seconds.
candidates.position: In consultations with older people, clinicians should sit facing the person with light on their own face, and should speak before or after typing, not while typing.
claims_needing_evidence: Seeing the talker's face substantially improves speech intelligibility in noise compared with listening alone (Sumby and Pollack 1954, J Acoust Soc Am; later audiovisual speech studies).
Older adults with hearing loss use visual speech cues to support understanding (audiology review; check).
Communication guidance for people with hearing loss advises facing the person, keeping light on the speaker's face and not covering the mouth (RNID or NHS communication guidance).
Hearing loss is common among people over 60 (WHO World report on hearing 2021; check the figure before quoting).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'compare the stated aim of a service with what happens', with the decade timescale, led to the Accessible Information Standard in England, in force for about a decade, and the small-print letters and phone calls that still reach people who are unable to read or hear them.
candidates.working_title: Ask them to record how you need to be contacted
candidates.core_insight: In England, NHS and adult social care services must identify, record, flag, share and meet the communication needs of people with sensory loss or disability, so you can ask your GP practice or hospital to record that you need, for example, large print, texts instead of calls, or a sign language interpreter.
candidates.angle: The standard sets out a clear aim. The person's experience can still be an appointment letter in small print, a phone call they did not hear, or a name called in a waiting room. Asking for the need to be recorded turns a private difficulty into a flag the next receptionist can see.
candidates.position: People in England with hearing or sight loss can ask services to record their communication needs under the Accessible Information Standard, and services should check that the flag changes what they send and do.
claims_needing_evidence: The Accessible Information Standard (DCB1605) requires NHS and publicly funded adult social care organisations in England to identify, record, flag, share and meet the information and communication needs of people with a disability, impairment or sensory loss (NHS England specification; check current version and any revision).
Organisations were required to comply by 31 July 2016 (NHS England; check).
Implementation has been incomplete (NHS England post-implementation review 2017 or Healthwatch reports; check before stating).
The standard applies in England only; other UK nations have different arrangements (check before mentioning).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'ask who bears the cost' led from the person with hearing loss to the partner who repeats things, relays phone calls and loses easy conversation, which researchers call third-party disability.
candidates.working_title: Hearing loss in a couple is shared
candidates.core_insight: Spouses of older people with hearing loss commonly report effects on their own lives, and bringing the partner into hearing care, including learning communication tactics together, helps both people.
candidates.angle: Hearing services measure the person's hearing. Part of the cost falls on the partner: in one study of 100 spouses, nearly all reported some degree of what researchers call third-party disability, mostly mild. That is a reason to bring the partner to the appointment and to agree tactics together, without making the partner the household's permanent interpreter.
candidates.position: Hearing assessment and rehabilitation should invite the communication partner, and both people's difficulties deserve attention.
claims_needing_evidence: In a study of 100 spouses of older people with hearing impairment, 98% reported some degree of third-party disability on at least one item, mostly mild (Scarinci, Worrall and Hickson 2012, Ear Hear; abstract read in PubMed).

Third-party disability means disability and functioning problems in family members arising from their relative's health condition, and was identified by WHO in the ICF framework as a direction for development (Scarinci et al. 2009, Disabil Rehabil; abstract read).

A group communication education programme for older people with hearing impairment (ACE) improved self-reported hearing handicap and communication in an RCT, maintained at 6 months (Hickson et al. 2007, Ear Hear; abstract read; check the role of significant others in the full text).
UK audiology guidance encourages a communication partner to attend appointments (NHS or British Society of Audiology source; check).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'examine a neglected consequence', with 'what is left over' and the first week, pointed to the old glasses that no longer suit the operated eye while a person waits for new glasses or surgery on the second eye.
candidates.working_title: Between the first and second cataract operation
candidates.core_insight: After cataract surgery on one eye, old glasses may no longer suit that eye, which can leave vision uneven until new glasses or the second operation; an optician can often remove or change the lens on the operated side, and it helps to ask before surgery what to do.
candidates.angle: The operation is judged a success in the operated eye. The person goes home to glasses made for an eye that has changed. The two eyes may now need very different lenses, and the gap can last weeks or months, stairs and kerbs included. A second-eye trial found better visual function and confidence after expedited surgery, while the effect on falls was uncertain.
candidates.position: Before first-eye cataract surgery, people should be told what to do about their glasses until the second eye or new glasses, and should ask if nobody has said.
claims_needing_evidence: After first-eye cataract surgery, a large difference in prescription between the two eyes can make existing glasses blurred or uncomfortable (ophthalmology source; check).

Patient information advises that new glasses are usually prescribed a few weeks after surgery and that the lens on the operated side may be removed or replaced in the meantime (NHS trust or RCOphth patient leaflet; check wording).

In an RCT of 239 women over 70, expedited second-eye cataract surgery improved visual function and confidence; the 32% lower rate of falling was not statistically significant (Foss et al. 2006, Age Ageing; abstract read in PubMed).
NICE NG77 recommends offering second-eye cataract surgery using the same criteria as first-eye surgery (NICE NG77; check wording).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'follow the event over time', with the first-month timescale and 'labelling', structured a timeline of sudden hearing loss in one ear, where the useful action is in the first days and the common delay comes from labelling it wax.
candidates.working_title: Sudden hearing loss in one ear needs seeing today
candidates.core_insight: Hearing that drops suddenly in one ear over hours to a few days needs same-day medical assessment, because sudden loss from the inner ear or nerve is treated as urgent and should not be assumed to be wax.
candidates.angle: Follow a common sequence: a blocked feeling on waking, a guess that it is wax, drops for a week, then a routine appointment. By then the period guidelines treat as urgent has passed. An examination and a tuning fork test can quickly separate a blocked ear canal from loss in the inner ear or nerve. Treatment evidence is uncertain, which is a reason for specialist assessment rather than for waiting.
candidates.position: Sudden hearing loss in one ear should be assessed the same day, rather than treated as wax at home.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE NG98 recommends immediate referral (to be seen within 24 hours) to ENT or an emergency department for adults with sudden onset hearing loss (developing over 3 days or less) within the past 30 days that is not explained by external or middle ear causes (NICE NG98 recommendation 1.1.1; check wording).
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is defined as a loss of at least 30 dB over at least three consecutive frequencies within 72 hours (AAO-HNS guideline, Chandrasekhar 2019).

Corticosteroids are often offered for sudden sensorineural hearing loss and, if used, are given early; evidence of benefit is uncertain (AAO-HNS 2019 guideline; Cochrane review of systemic steroids; check).
The Weber and Rinne tuning fork tests help distinguish conductive from sensorineural hearing loss (clinical examination text).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find an outcome that patients value and the routine measure misses', with postal delivery, the wall calendar, 'permission' and the occupational therapist at discharge, led to reading your own letters privately, which standard independence scores leave out.
candidates.working_title: Reading your own post
candidates.core_insight: Standard measures of independence such as the Barthel Index have no item on reading, yet for a person with sight loss, reading their own letters, bank statements and medicine labels privately is part of independence that low vision services can often restore with magnifiers, lighting and reading apps.
candidates.angle: A person can score as fully independent in washing, dressing and walking and still need someone else to open and read every letter, including bank and hospital letters. That loss of privacy and control is not recorded. Low vision assessments work from the tasks the person chooses, and reading post is a common one.
candidates.position: Assessments of older people with sight loss should ask whether they can read their own post and medicine labels, and refer to low vision services when they are unable to.
claims_needing_evidence: The Barthel Index has 10 items (feeding, bathing, grooming, dressing, bowels, bladder, toilet use, transfers, mobility, stairs) and none on reading or communication (Mahoney and Barthel 1965; Collin et al. 1988).
Low vision rehabilitation improves visual reading ability in people with low vision (LOVIT trial, Stelmack et al. 2008; Cochrane review of reading aids; check).
NHS low vision services provide assessment, magnifiers and advice, usually free of charge (NHS or College of Optometrists source; check).
Phone apps can magnify text or read printed text aloud (general product information; do not name brands).

candidates.working_title: Is hearing the last sense to go?
candidates.core_insight: A small study of brain recordings found that many unresponsive people close to death still showed brain responses to sounds, which suggests hearing may keep working in some people near the end of life, though it does not show they understood; it is reasonable for families to keep speaking to the person.

The practical detail follows without overclaiming: say who you are, speak to the person rather than about them, and, while it is comfortable, keep a hearing aid in.

These brain responses do not establish conscious understanding; the MMN is considered automatic (Blundon 2020; abstract read).
Care guidance for the last days of life advises continuing to talk to the dying person and explaining care (NICE NG31 or palliative care patient information; check wording).

candidates.working_title: Loud enough, still unclear
candidates.core_insight: Age-related hearing loss usually affects high-pitched sounds first, and these carry consonants such as s, f, th and t, so speech can be loud enough to hear but hard to understand; shouting does not fix this, while facing the person, getting their attention and rephrasing help.
candidates.angle: Families say 'she hears when she wants to'. The pattern has a physical explanation: vowels are lower-pitched and louder, consonants higher and softer, and age-related loss removes high pitches first. So the person hears that someone is speaking but mishears 'fifteen' as 'fifty'. Rephrasing in different words gives a second chance with different sounds; repeating the same words louder does not.
candidates.position: Families should replace shouting and repeating with facing the person, getting their attention first and rephrasing.
claims_needing_evidence: Age-related hearing loss (presbycusis) typically begins at, and is greatest at, high frequencies (Gates and Mills 2005, Lancet review).
Consonants carry more high-frequency energy and less intensity than vowels and contribute strongly to speech understanding (audiology or phonetics text; check).
Shouting distorts speech and does not improve understanding for people with age-related hearing loss (audiology guidance; check source).
Communication guidance advises rephrasing rather than repeating when someone has not understood (RNID guidance).

candidates.working_title: Hearing aids for hearing: what ACHIEVE found about memory
candidates.core_insight: In the ACHIEVE trial, hearing aids with audiology support did not reduce cognitive decline over three years in the whole group, with a possible difference in a higher-risk subgroup, so hearing aids should be recommended for their clear benefit to hearing and communication, and any effect on dementia described as unproven.
candidates.angle: Hearing loss appears on dementia prevention lists because of observational links. ACHIEVE tested the idea in 977 people aged 70 to 84 over three years and found no difference in the primary outcome. A prespecified analysis suggested a difference in an older, higher-risk cohort; that is a hypothesis to test. Meanwhile the benefit for hearing is well established. Recommending hearing aids mainly as dementia prevention risks disappointment when memory still declines.
candidates.position: Clinicians should recommend hearing aids for hearing and communication, and describe any effect on dementia risk as unproven.
claims_needing_evidence: ACHIEVE randomised 977 adults aged 70 to 84 with untreated hearing loss to a hearing intervention or health education; 3-year change in global cognition did not differ (difference 0.002 SD units, p=0.96) (Lin et al. 2023, Lancet; abstract read in PubMed).
A prespecified sensitivity analysis found a different effect in the ARIC cohort, who were older with more risk factors, than in the community volunteers (Lin et al. 2023; abstract read).
The Lancet Commission lists hearing loss as a potentially modifiable dementia risk factor, based mainly on observational studies (Livingston et al. 2024, Lancet).
The 2026 Cochrane update found very uncertain evidence for an effect of hearing aids on working memory and likely large benefits for listening (Ferguson et al. 2026; abstract read).

candidates.working_title: Eye drops that slow the heart
candidates.core_insight: Beta-blocker eye drops such as timolol are absorbed into the bloodstream and can cause a slow heart rate, heart block, fainting and breathlessness, so they belong in every medicines review for bradycardia, syncope and falls.
candidates.angle: Eye drops rarely appear on the list of suspects for a slow pulse or a blackout. Drops drain through the tear duct into the nose and are absorbed there without passing through the liver first. Case reports describe heart block and fainting that resolved when the drops stopped. Pressing on the inner corner of the eye after the drop reduces absorption, and other glaucoma drops exist.
candidates.position: In an older person with bradycardia, syncope, falls or new breathlessness, ask specifically about eye drops, and discuss alternatives with the eye team if a beta-blocker drop may be responsible.
claims_needing_evidence: Topical timolol enters the systemic circulation and produces systemic beta-blockade (BNF or SPC; Wang et al. 2019, BMC Pharmacol Toxicol; abstract read in PubMed).
Case reports describe complete heart block, symptomatic bradyarrhythmia and syncope attributed to timolol eye drops that resolved on stopping (Wang 2019; Prodolliet 2025; Eyal 2015; abstracts read).

Nasolacrimal occlusion and a tissue press method each reduced plasma timolol concentration compared with no intervention in a cross-over trial (Müller et al. 2019, Clin Exp Ophthalmol; abstract read).

candidates.working_title: Seeing things after sight loss
candidates.core_insight: People with sight loss, for example from macular degeneration, can see vivid images such as faces, patterns or people that are not there while knowing they are not real; this is Charles Bonnet syndrome, it is linked to the sight loss, and it is worth mentioning to a doctor so other causes can be considered.

claims_needing_evidence: Charles Bonnet syndrome is complex visual hallucinations in people with visual impairment who keep insight (Teunisse et al. 1996, Lancet; abstract read in PubMed).

candidates.working_title: New glasses, more falls: a trial worth knowing
candidates.core_insight: In a Sydney trial of frail older people, eye examinations with new glasses and other treatment increased falls rather than reducing them, which suggests that changes to glasses in frail people need care and a settling-in period.

candidates.working_title: When hearing and sight both fade
candidates.core_insight: When a person has both hearing and sight loss, each sense can no longer make up for the other (lip-reading needs sight; getting about with poor sight relies on hearing), so the combination needs an assessment by someone who understands both.
candidates.angle: Services are organised by organ: audiology in one building, the eye clinic in another. A person with both losses loses the usual workarounds. They are unable to lip-read a face they do not see clearly, or to hear traffic they do not see. In England, statutory guidance requires councils to identify people with combined sight and hearing loss and to arrange a specialist assessment.
candidates.position: Anyone assessing an older person's hearing should ask about sight, and the reverse; people with both should be offered a specialist dual sensory loss assessment.
claims_needing_evidence: Dual sensory impairment is common in older people and becomes more common with age (Heine and Browning 2002 review; UK estimates from Sense; check).
People with hearing loss rely on visual cues for speech, which sight loss reduces (Heine and Browning 2002; check).

In England, the Care and support for deafblind children and adults policy guidance (Department of Health 2014, under the Care Act) requires councils to identify, contact and keep a record of deafblind people and to ensure an assessment by a specifically trained person (check wording).
In Scotland, the See Hear framework (Scottish Government 2014) covers services for people with sensory impairment, including dual sensory loss (check).
In a study of 301 older adults, 7% had dual sensory impairment (Dupuis et al. 2015; abstract read).

candidates.gain: A term to use and an assessment to ask for.
candidates.follow: It speaks up for people whose needs services split apart.

candidates.working_title: Changes in sight that need an appointment today
candidates.core_insight: Sudden loss or blurring of sight, a shadow or curtain across vision, new flashes or a shower of floaters, straight lines that look wavy, or sight problems with a new headache and scalp tenderness need to be seen the same day rather than at the next routine sight test.
candidates.angle: Older people are used to eyesight changing slowly and to booking a sight test for it. A few changes are time-critical: retinal detachment, wet macular degeneration, giant cell arteritis and stroke affecting the eye. Each has a pattern a person can recognise. The useful sentence on the phone is specific: 'I have new flashes and a shadow in my vision. I need to be seen today.'
candidates.position: People should know these symptoms and seek same-day help from an optometrist, eye casualty or NHS 111 (NHS 24 in Scotland), and call 999 for sudden loss of sight with stroke signs.
claims_needing_evidence: New flashes, a sudden shower of floaters, or a shadow or curtain across vision can indicate a retinal tear or detachment, which needs urgent assessment (NICE CKS retinal detachment; RCOphth; check).

Distortion, such as straight lines looking wavy, or sudden central vision loss can indicate wet age-related macular degeneration, and NICE NG82 recommends urgent referral to a macular service (check the timeframe).

In people over 50, a new headache with scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing or visual symptoms suggests giant cell arteritis, which can cause permanent sight loss and needs same-day assessment (BSR 2020 guideline).
Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye, including brief loss, can be a transient ischaemic attack or retinal artery occlusion and needs emergency stroke assessment (NICE NG128; check).

NICE NG128. Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management (2019)

candidates.follow: Practical safety information in plain words.

candidates.working_title: Suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms: treat today
candidates.core_insight: In suspected giant cell arteritis, especially with visual symptoms, glucocorticoids should start immediately and the person be assessed urgently by a specialist, because sight loss may be permanent, and ultrasound or biopsy can still be done after treatment starts.
candidates.angle: The common delay is waiting for inflammatory markers, a biopsy date or a clinic slot before starting steroids. The BSR guideline advises starting glucocorticoids on strong suspicion, before confirmation, with urgent referral to a fast-track pathway; ultrasound and biopsy stay informative for a limited period after treatment starts. In older people the story can be vague: tiredness, weight loss, jaw ache when chewing.
candidates.position: Start glucocorticoids on clinical suspicion of giant cell arteritis and refer to a fast-track pathway the same day, without waiting for test results.
claims_needing_evidence: The BSR 2020 guideline recommends immediate glucocorticoid treatment when giant cell arteritis is strongly suspected, before the diagnosis is confirmed, with urgent specialist referral (Mackie et al. 2020, Rheumatology).
Visual loss from giant cell arteritis is usually permanent (BSR 2020 guideline; review).
Temporal artery ultrasound and biopsy remain informative for a limited period after glucocorticoids start (BSR 2020; check the stated time windows).
The BSR guideline recommends a higher starting dose, or intravenous methylprednisolone, for people with visual symptoms (check exact recommendation).
Features include new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual disturbance, and systemic symptoms may dominate in older people (BSR 2020).

NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: giant cell arteritis

candidates.follow: Direct teaching on time-critical conditions in older people.

candidates.working_title: Dizzy when rolling over in bed: test for BPPV
candidates.core_insight: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (brief spinning set off by lying down, rolling over or looking up) is common and often unrecognised in older people, can be diagnosed with the Dix-Hallpike test, and is often treatable within minutes with a repositioning manoeuvre.
candidates.angle: Dizziness in older people is often filed as multifactorial and treated with sedating tablets. In an inner-city geriatric clinic population, 9% had unrecognised BPPV, and they were more likely to have fallen in the previous three months. Asking what sets the dizziness off, and doing a Dix-Hallpike test, turns a vague complaint into a diagnosis with a treatment.
candidates.position: Older people with dizziness should be asked about positional triggers and examined with the Dix-Hallpike test before being given a non-specific label or vestibular sedatives.
claims_needing_evidence: In a cross-sectional study of an inner-city geriatric population, 9% had unrecognised BPPV, which was associated with lower ADL scores, a fall in the previous 3 months and depression (Oghalai et al. 2000, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg; abstract read in PubMed).
The Dix-Hallpike test diagnoses posterior canal BPPV and the Epley manoeuvre is an effective treatment (AAO-HNS BPPV guideline, Bhattacharyya 2017; Cochrane review, Hilton and Pinder 2014).
Guidelines advise against routine vestibular suppressant medicines for BPPV (AAO-HNS 2017).
Prochlorperazine can cause drowsiness and movement side effects in older people (BNF).

candidates.gain: A question, a test and a treatment.
candidates.follow: Bedside skills that change outcomes.

candidates.working_title: The vision screening that did not improve vision
candidates.core_insight: In a large UK trial of people aged 75 and over, adding vision screening to health checks did not improve eyesight three to five years later, which shows that finding eye problems helps only when treatment such as glasses or cataract surgery follows.
candidates.angle: Screening programmes are often counted by people tested and referred. The Smeeth trial counted something harder: whether eyesight was better years later. It was not. Possible reasons include problems already known to the person, referrals not taken up, and conditions without effective treatment at the time. The useful count for any detection programme is sight corrected.
candidates.position: Programmes to find sight problems in older people should be judged by whether sight is corrected, and should make the step from detection to treatment easy.
claims_needing_evidence: In a cluster RCT of 4340 people aged 75 and over in 20 UK general practices, universal vision screening compared with targeted screening did not change the proportion with visual acuity below 6/18 or visual function scores 3 to 5 years later (Smeeth et al. 2003, BMJ; abstract read in PubMed).
The trial report discusses low uptake of referral and already-known problems as explanations (full text; check).
A Cochrane review of community vision screening in older people found no improvement in vision outcomes (Clarke, Evans and Smeeth 2018; check).
Uncorrected refractive error and cataract are leading causes of visual impairment in older people in Britain (Evans et al. 2004, Br J Ophthalmol; check).

candidates.working_title: Tell the audiologist where you want to hear better
candidates.core_insight: Some hearing services ask you to name up to five situations where you most want to hear better, such as a grandchild on the phone or a lunch club, and then judge success against those, so thinking about them before the appointment helps.
candidates.angle: A hearing test measures the quietest sounds you can detect in a soundproof booth. What you may want is to follow the conversation at the family table. The Client Oriented Scale of Improvement turns the person's own goals into the measure of success. It is a small example of care organised around what the person values, and it works best when the person arrives with a list.
candidates.position: Before a hearing appointment, write down the situations where you most want to hear better, and ask for your progress to be judged against them.
claims_needing_evidence: The COSI asks the client to name up to five listening situations where help is needed, and measures improvement in those situations after rehabilitation (Dillon, James and Ginis 1997, J Am Acad Audiol; abstract read in PubMed).
The COSI performed as well statistically as longer questionnaires and suits routine clinical use (Dillon 1997; abstract read).
UK audiology services use goal-based outcome tools such as the COSI or the Glasgow Hearing Aid Benefit Profile (British Academy of Audiology or NHS source; check).
Pure-tone audiometry measures hearing thresholds in a sound-treated room and does not measure understanding of speech in noise (audiology text).

candidates.working_title: A fading sense of smell is a safety issue
candidates.core_insight: The sense of smell declines with age, so many older people may not notice gas, smoke or food that has gone off, and working alarms, date labels and timers take over the warning job.
candidates.angle: Smell is rarely asked about. In a large 1984 study, more than half of people aged 65 to 80, and more than three quarters of those over 80, had major loss of smell identification. In a smell clinic cohort, people with impaired smell were about twice as likely to report a hazardous event such as a cooking accident, eating spoiled food or missing a gas leak. The fixes are ordinary and cheap.
candidates.position: Older people and families should ask about sense of smell and make sure smoke, gas and carbon monoxide alarms are fitted and working, rather than relying on smell.
claims_needing_evidence: Smell identification declines markedly after the seventh decade; more than half of people aged 65 to 80, and more than three quarters over 80, had major olfactory impairment (Doty et al. 1984, Science; abstract read in PubMed).

In a retrospective cohort of 445 smell clinic patients, 37% with impaired smell and 19% with normal smell reported at least one smell-related hazardous event, most often cooking incidents, spoiled food and undetected gas leaks (Santos et al. 2004, Arch Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg; abstract read).
Many older people with smell loss are unaware of it (study comparing self-report with testing; check).
Carbon monoxide has no smell, so a carbon monoxide alarm is needed regardless of sense of smell (HSE or Gas Safe Register source).

candidates.working_title: For many Deaf people who sign, English is a second language
candidates.core_insight: Many Deaf people who use British Sign Language have English as a second language, so written notes and lip-reading are poor substitutes for a qualified BSL interpreter in health and care, and relatives should not be asked to interpret.
candidates.angle: Staff often reach for a pen and paper. For a person who grew up Deaf and signs, written English may be much weaker than their BSL. A UK study of Deaf BSL users found more unrecognised high blood pressure and poorer control of treated high blood pressure than in the general population, consistent with poor access to care. An older Deaf person in a care home may be the only person there who signs.
candidates.position: Health and care services should book qualified BSL interpreters for Deaf BSL users, including in care homes, rather than relying on writing, lip-reading or relatives.
claims_needing_evidence: BSL is a language in its own right, recognised in law by the British Sign Language (Scotland) Act 2015 and the British Sign Language Act 2022 (legislation).
Many Deaf BSL users have English as a second language and lower English literacy (research on Deaf literacy or SignHealth report; check).

In a UK sample of 298 Deaf BSL users, 37% had high blood pressure readings vs 21% in the Health Survey for England, 29% were unaware vs 6%, and 42% of those treated had adequate control vs 62% (Emond et al. 2015, BMJ Open; abstract read in PubMed).
NHS England guidance advises against using family members as interpreters except in emergencies (NHS England 2018 guidance on interpreting in primary care; check wording).
Older Deaf BSL users in care homes can be isolated where no one signs (qualitative study; check).

candidates.working_title: A cognitive test is also a hearing and vision test
candidates.core_insight: Cognitive screening tests are delivered by voice and on paper, so hearing or sight loss can lower scores; check the person can hear and see the items, use aids and simple adaptations, and record them with the score.
candidates.angle: A person who mishears the words in a recall task scores as if they forgot them. In a study of 301 older adults, more people with normal hearing and vision passed the MoCA than people with sensory loss, even after score adjustments. Practical adaptations exist: hearing aids in, a personal amplifier, a room without background noise, large print, written copies of spoken instructions, and versions of tests designed for people with hearing loss.
candidates.position: Before any cognitive screen, check hearing and vision, use aids and adaptations, and write down which were used alongside the score.
claims_needing_evidence: In 301 older adults, more participants with normal sensory acuity passed the MoCA than those with sensory loss, even after modifying scores to adjust for sensory factors (Dupuis et al. 2015, Aging Neuropsychol Cogn; abstract read in PubMed).
Many standard cognitive tests include items that must be heard or seen (Dupuis 2015; abstract read).
A version of the MoCA for people with severe hearing loss (HI-MoCA or MoCA-H) has been developed (Lin VYW et al. 2017, Laryngoscope; check).
Hearing impairment lowers performance on verbally administered cognitive tests (systematic review, e.g. Utoomprurkporn et al. 2020; check).

candidates.working_title: Cataract surgery when a person has dementia
candidates.core_insight: People with dementia can benefit from cataract surgery through better recognition of faces, activities and safer movement, and the decision turns on practical questions (lying still, the type of anaesthetic, weeks of eye drops, not rubbing the eye) that need planning with the person and their family.
candidates.angle: Two opposite errors are possible: assuming a person with dementia will not benefit, and operating without a plan for after-care. The useful questions are specific. Will better sight help what this person does and enjoys? Can they lie still under local anaesthetic, or is sedation or a general anaesthetic needed? Who will give the drops, and will they tolerate an eye shield at night? The evidence is limited and mostly observational, so the decision rests on the person.
candidates.position: Cataract surgery should be considered on its merits for people with dementia, with a plan for anaesthesia and after-care made with the person and their family.
claims_needing_evidence: Cataract and dementia commonly coexist in older people, and visual impairment may worsen function in dementia (Jefferis et al. 2011, Br J Ophthalmol review; check).
Observational studies report improved visual function and some quality of life measures after cataract surgery in people with cognitive impairment (review; check).

Cataract surgery is usually done under local anaesthesia and requires the person to lie still for [N to verify] minutes; sedation or general anaesthesia can be used when this is not possible (RCOphth or Royal College of Anaesthetists guidance; check).
After cataract surgery, eye drops are usually used several times a day for several weeks (NHS patient information; check regimen).
NICE NG97 advises that people with dementia should not be excluded from services because of their diagnosis (check wording).
